More than half of Indonesia's provinces are an island name plus a
compass word, so the compass words do most of the work:
utara = north    selatan = south    barat = west    timur = east
So Sumatera Utara is North Sumatra, Kalimantan Timur is East Borneo,
Sulawesi Tenggara is South-East Sulawesi. Learn those six words and
about twenty of the thirty-three names read themselves; the hook for
those is the island's own name, which is the interesting part.
Ids follow the map's spelling, so Java is 'jawa' and Jakarta is
aceh: The name's origin is disputed; one old story has it as an acronym of the Arab, Chinese, European and Hindu traders who met here.
Called the veranda of Mecca: Islam entered the archipelago through this port, and it is the only province under sharia law.
The 2004 tsunami killed about 170,000 people here, and the disaster ended a thirty-year separatist war within a year.
sulawesi-utara: North Sulawesi — the island's own name probably comes from sula besi, "iron island", for the metal traded from it.
Its Minahasan people are largely Christian and its cuisine is the spiciest in Indonesia, with dishes other Indonesians find alarming.
Bunaken off its coast drops to 1,500 m just offshore, which is why its wall diving is world famous.
sumatera-utara: North Sumatra; Sumatra itself may come from samudra, Sanskrit for ocean, through an old kingdom's name.
Lake Toba here fills the caldera of a supervolcano that erupted about 74,000 years ago — the largest eruption in two million years.
The Batak peoples around that lake have their own script and were converted by German missionaries in the 1860s.
kepulauan-riau: "The Riau islands" — kepulauan means archipelago, and Riau may come from a Portuguese or local word for a river mouth.
Batam in it sits 20 km from Singapore and was developed as a free-trade rival to it.
The province is about 96% sea, with some 2,400 islands scattered across it.
kalimantan-timur: East Borneo — Kalimantan is the Indonesian name for the island, possibly from a word for raw sago or for the Kalamantan people.
Indonesia's new capital, Nusantara, is being built here to take the pressure off a sinking Jakarta.
Its coal and gas made it one of the richest provinces per head, and the Mahakam river through it holds a rare freshwater dolphin.
riau: The mainland half of the same Riau name, on Sumatra's east coast.
It produces much of Indonesia's oil and a large share of its palm oil.
The haze from its peatland fires regularly closes airports and schools in Singapore and Malaysia.
gorontalo: Probably from hulontalangi, "a more valuable land", or from a word for a place that floods.
Split from North Sulawesi in 2000; it is one of Indonesia's newest provinces and is Muslim-majority in a largely Christian neighbourhood.
Its whale sharks gather close to shore at Botubarani, where fishermen feed them by hand.
maluku-utara: North Maluku — the Moluccas, from Arabic jazirat al-muluk, "island of the kings", for its sultans.
These were the original Spice Islands: cloves and nutmeg grew here and nowhere else, which is what brought Europe to Asia.
Ternate and Tidore, two volcanic cones a few kilometres apart, were rival sultanates that between them controlled the world clove supply.
kalimantan-barat: The equator runs through Pontianak, its capital, which has a monument where the sun casts no shadow twice a year.
Its Kapuas is Indonesia's longest river at 1,143 km, and the province holds large orangutan populations.
sulawesi-tengah: The Bada valley in it has hundreds of megalithic stone figures whose carvers and purpose are unknown.
Palu was hit in 2018 by an earthquake, tsunami and soil liquefaction at once, which swallowed whole neighbourhoods.
sumatera-barat: Its Minangkabau are the largest matrilineal society in the world: property and family name pass through the mother.
Their houses have roofs curved like buffalo horns, and rendang, often voted the world's tastiest dish, is their cooking.
kalimantan-tengah: Created in 1957 after Dayak protests at being governed from the coast; it is the largest province by area on the island.
Tanjung Puting in it is the best-known place to see wild orangutans, reached by river boat.
jambi: Possibly from Javanese jambe, the areca palm, or from a local word for a place to ford.
The Srivijaya-era temple complex at Muaro Jambi is the largest ancient site in Indonesia, larger than Borobudur in area.
Kerinci in it is Sumatra's highest volcano at 3,805 m, and the forest around it holds the Sumatran tiger.
papua-barat: West Papua — Papua may come from a Malay word for frizzy hair, or from a Tidore phrase meaning "not joining".
Raja Ampat off its coast has the highest recorded coral and reef-fish diversity of anywhere on earth.
Its interior holds peoples contacted only in the twentieth century, and hundreds of languages.
sulawesi-barat: West Sulawesi, split from the south in 2004.
The Mandar people here build sandeq sailing boats with outriggers, among the fastest traditional sailing craft in the world.
It is one of the least populated and least visited provinces on the island.
bangka-belitung: Two islands: Bangka may be from a word for tin, which is exactly what it produces.
They have supplied tin for over two centuries, and much of the world's solder has passed through them.
Belitung's granite boulders on white sand were made famous by the novel and film Laskar Pelangi.
kalimantan-selatan: Banjarmasin in it is built on water, with floating markets where traders sell from canoes at dawn.
Its Meratus mountains hold Dayak communities, and the province mines a large share of Indonesia's coal.
sumatera-selatan: Palembang, its capital, was the seat of Srivijaya, a maritime empire that dominated the region from the 600s to the 1200s.
The Ampera bridge there used to lift in the middle to let ships pass; the lifting mechanism was removed in 1970.
bengkulu: Possibly from bangkahulu, "the place where the head is" — a reference to an old battle.
The British held it as Bencoolen for 140 years and swapped it for Singapore in 1824.
Rafflesia arnoldii, the largest single flower in the world at a metre across, was found here and is the provincial emblem.
sulawesi-selatan: Its Bugis were the great sailors of the archipelago, and their pinisi ships, still built by hand on the beach, are a UNESCO heritage item.
Toraja in its highlands holds funerals lasting days, with cliff graves and carved wooden effigies watching from the rock.
sulawesi-tenggara: The Wakatobi islands off it sit in the middle of the Coral Triangle and are a national marine park.
Its nickel is a large share of the world supply, which the electric-car industry has made suddenly strategic.
lampung: Possibly from lappung, meaning high or elevated, in the local language.
Krakatoa lies in the strait off it; the 1883 eruption was heard 4,800 km away and dropped global temperatures for years.
Its Way Kambas park runs an elephant school for the Sumatran elephant, and the province was the main destination of Java's transmigration programme.
papua: The larger, eastern part of Indonesian New Guinea.
Puncak Jaya here is the highest peak between the Himalaya and the Andes at 4,884 m, and carries glaciers on the equator — now nearly gone.
The Baliem valley was unknown to the outside world until an aircraft spotted its farmed terraces and 50,000 inhabitants in 1938.
maluku: The southern Moluccas, sharing the "island of the kings" name with the north.
Banda in it was the only source of nutmeg in the world; the Dutch massacred most of its population in 1621 to control the trade.
England traded its claim on Run, one of the Banda islands, to the Dutch in 1667 in exchange for Manhattan.
jakarta-raya: "Greater Jakarta" — the city's name is from Jayakarta, "complete victory", given in 1527; the Dutch renamed it Batavia and Indonesia changed it back in 1942.
It is sinking up to 25 cm a year in the north, faster than almost any other city, which is why the capital is moving to Borneo.
Its metropolitan area is among the largest in the world, around 30 million people.
banten: Named for the sultanate of Banten, a pepper port powerful enough that the first English and Dutch fleets came here before anywhere else.
The Baduy people in its hills reject modern technology by choice, and the inner group allows no vehicles, footwear or money.
jawa-barat: West Java — Java's own name may come from Sanskrit yava, barley or grain.
The most populous province in Indonesia, with about 50 million people.
Its Sundanese are the country's second-largest ethnic group, with their own language and a gamelan quite unlike the Javanese one.
jawa-tengah: Borobudur here is the largest Buddhist temple in the world, built around 800 and abandoned within 150 years; Prambanan nearby is its Hindu counterpart.
Javanese court culture — batik, gamelan, wayang shadow puppets — all comes from this region, and all three are UNESCO heritage items.
jawa-timur: Mount Bromo in it sits inside a sea of volcanic sand, and the Tenggerese throw offerings into its crater each year.
Surabaya, its capital, is where the independence fighting of November 1945 took place, commemorated as Heroes' Day.
yogyakarta: From Ayodhya, the city in the Ramayana, plus karta, prosperous — "a fit and prosperous Ayodhya".
The only Indonesian region still ruled by its monarchy: the sultan is governor by right, not election.
It was the capital of the republic during the independence war, and is the country's student and arts city.
bali: Possibly from Sanskrit wali, an offering — which suits an island whose households make them daily.
The only Hindu-majority province, because Javanese nobility and priests fled here when Islam spread in the 1500s.
Its subak irrigation system, run by temple councils for over a thousand years, is a UNESCO site.
nusa-tenggara-barat: "West south-eastern islands" — nusa is island, tenggara south-east.
Lombok's Rinjani is Indonesia's second-highest volcano, with a crater lake and a cone growing inside it.
Sumbawa next door produced the 1815 Tambora eruption, the largest in recorded history, which caused Europe's year without a summer.
nusa-tenggara-timur: The eastern half of the same island chain.
Komodo dragons live here and nowhere else — up to 3 m long, and only described by science in 1910.
It is the only Christian-majority province outside eastern Indonesia's Papua and Maluku, and its Sumba island keeps a megalithic burial tradition.
banda-aceh: "Port of Aceh" — bandar is a port, a Persian word that spread across the Muslim trading world.
The 2004 tsunami killed about a quarter of the city’s people; a ship carried inland by the wave is left where it landed.
Its Baiturrahman mosque survived the wave and sheltered survivors.
binjai: Named for the binjai, a mango relative that grows in Sumatra.
A plantation town near Medan, growing rubber and oil palm.
It sits at the edge of the Leuser ecosystem, one of the last places where orangutans, tigers, rhinos and elephants live together.
medan: From a Malay word for a field or an open place — or possibly from Tamil maidan.
It grew on tobacco: Deli leaf from here was the world’s best cigar wrapper.
It is Indonesia’s fourth largest city and has large Tamil and Chinese communities.
tebingtinggi: "High cliff" — tebing a cliff, tinggi high.
A rail junction between Medan and the plantation belt.
It sits on the road to Lake Toba, the supervolcano caldera.
pematangsiantar: From pematang, a raised ridge or dyke, plus Siantar, a local name.
It is the main town of the Simalungun Batak and has one of Indonesia’s oldest zoos.
Its becak are powered by vintage BSA motorcycles left behind after the war.
sibolga: Of Batak origin, possibly from a phrase about a bay.
A small port on the Indian Ocean, and the ferry point for Nias island.
Nias, offshore, has megalithic villages and a stone-jumping tradition performed over 2 m walls.
manado: From a Minahasan word, possibly "on the coast" or the name of an island.
Bunaken off it drops to 1,500 m just offshore, which is why its wall diving is world famous.
Its Minahasan cooking is the spiciest in Indonesia, with dishes other Indonesians approach carefully.
padangsidempuan: "The field of Sidempuan" — padang is a field or plain.
It is the main town of the southern Batak region and is known for its salak fruit.
It sits in a valley ringed by hills, on the Trans-Sumatran highway.
tanjungpinang: "Pinang cape" — tanjung a cape, pinang the areca palm.
It was the seat of the Riau-Lingga sultanate, and standard Malay — the basis of Indonesian — was codified in this area.
Penyengat island beside it has a mosque said to be mortared with egg white.
singkawang: From Hakka Chinese san kew jong, "a town of hills, sea and estuary".
It has the highest proportion of Chinese-descended residents of any Indonesian city, about a third.
Its Cap Go Meh festival, fifteen days after Chinese New Year, is the largest in the country.
pekanbaru: "New market" — pekan a market, baru new.
The centre of Indonesia’s oil industry, near the Duri and Minas fields.
The Japanese built a railway through here in 1944-45 with forced labour; thousands died and it was never used.
pontianak: Named for a vampiric ghost of Malay folklore — the founding sultan is said to have been harassed by one.
The equator runs through the city, marked by a monument where the sun casts no shadow twice a year.
It sits at the fork of the Kapuas, Indonesia’s longest river.
bukittinggi: "High hill" — bukit a hill, tinggi high.
It was the capital of the emergency government of Indonesia in 1948-49 when the Dutch captured the leadership.
Its Japanese tunnel system, dug by forced labour in 1942, runs for kilometres under the town.
samarinda: From sama rendah, "equally low" — the founding Buginese settlers built houses all at the same height to show equality.
It is the capital of East Kalimantan and sits on the Mahakam river.
Indonesia’s new capital, Nusantara, is being built in its province.
palu: From a local word meaning a place that has been levelled, or a bay.
The 2018 earthquake, tsunami and soil liquefaction here swallowed whole neighbourhoods.
Its bay is unusually deep and narrow, which amplified the wave.
padang: Padang food, served by bringing every dish to the table and charging only for what is eaten, is the most widespread regional cuisine in Indonesia.
Rendang, from this region, is regularly voted one of the world’s best dishes.
balikpapan: From a legend about a plank, balik papan, that floated back to shore.
The oil city of Borneo, with a refinery running since 1922.
It is regularly rated the cleanest and most liveable city in Kalimantan.
palembang: From limbang, to pan for gold, with the pe- prefix — a place where things are washed.
It was the capital of Srivijaya, a maritime empire that dominated the region from the 600s to the 1200s.
Its Ampera bridge used to lift in the middle for ships; the mechanism was removed in 1970.
banjarmasin: From banjar, a row of settlements, plus masih, a local chief’s name.
It is built on water, with floating markets where traders sell from canoes at dawn.
It is called the city of a thousand rivers, and much of it is below sea level.
martapura: "City of jewels" — from Sanskrit marta plus pura, a city.
It is the diamond-trading centre of Indonesia, with stones dug by hand from river gravel at Cempaka.
The Trisakti diamond, 166 carats, was found nearby in 1965.
majene: Of Mandar origin; the town is the historic seat of the Mandar people.
Its sandeq sailing boats with outriggers are among the fastest traditional sailing craft in the world.
It is the cultural centre of West Sulawesi, with a museum of Mandar seafaring.
ambon: Possibly from ambong, a Malay word for dew, or from a local name.
It was the Dutch East India Company’s first headquarters in the archipelago, before Batavia.
The 1623 Amboyna massacre of English traders here ended English ambitions in the Spice Islands and pushed them towards India.
makassar: Of local origin; it was Ujung Pandang from 1971 to 1999 before reverting.
Its Bugis and Makassar sailors ranged as far as northern Australia, trading with Aboriginal people for centuries.
The oil used on Victorian hair gave English the word antimacassar, for the cloth protecting chair backs.
bandar-lampung: "Port of Lampung" — bandar a port, the same Persian word as in Banda Aceh.
Krakatoa is in the strait off it; the 1883 eruption destroyed the towns it was formed from.
It is the gateway between Sumatra and Java, with ferries across the Sunda Strait.
jakarta: From Jayakarta, "complete victory", given in 1527; the Dutch renamed it Batavia and Indonesia changed it back in 1942.
It is sinking up to 25 cm a year in the north, faster than almost any other city.
That is why the capital is being moved to Borneo, a decision taken in 2019.
bekasi: From Sanskrit candrabhaga, a river name — the same root as Chenab in Pakistan.
It is one of Indonesia’s largest industrial zones and part of Greater Jakarta.
Its population has grown roughly tenfold since 1980.
bogor: From a Sundanese word for the sugar palm, or possibly "tree stump".
It has more thunderstorms than almost anywhere on earth, about 320 days a year, and is called the rain city.
Its botanical garden, founded 1817, is one of the oldest in the tropics and where oil palm was first grown in Asia.
cirebon: From caruban, "a mixture", or from ci-rebon, "shrimp water" — the town made shrimp paste.
Its palaces mix Javanese, Chinese, Islamic and European design, reflecting that mixture.
Its batik, in a cloud pattern called megamendung, is a distinct style.
tegal: From a Javanese word for a dry field.
Its warung tegal, cheap eating stalls, are found all over Jakarta and are an institution.
It has made metal goods since Dutch times and is nicknamed the Japan of Indonesia for its workshops.
pekalongan: Possibly from a word about a harvest or an abundance.
It is a UNESCO Creative City for its batik, and its patterns absorbed Chinese, Arab and Dutch influences.
Its batik museum holds pieces going back two centuries.
sukabumi: "Pleasant land" — suka pleasure, bumi earth, in Sundanese.
It sits below Mount Gede and was a Dutch hill retreat from Batavia.
The world’s oldest known geothermal drilling in Asia took place nearby in 1926.
bandung: From bendung, a dam — a lake formed by a lava flow once filled the basin.
The 1955 Asian-African Conference here founded the Non-Aligned Movement.
It is called the Paris of Java for its art deco buildings and its cool highland climate.
semarang: Its Lawang Sewu, "a thousand doors", was the Dutch railway headquarters and is the city’s landmark.
Admiral Zheng He’s fleet landed nearby in the 1400s, and a temple marks the spot.
surabaya: From suro, a shark, and boyo, a crocodile — the two are on the city arms, fighting.
The independence fighting of November 1945 here is commemorated as Heroes’ Day.
It is Indonesia’s second city and its main eastern port.
tasikmalaya: From tasik, a lake, plus malaya, a range of hills.
It is known for handicrafts: umbrellas, embroidery and woven pandan mats.
It is one of the most devoutly Muslim towns in West Java, with many pesantren schools.
surakarta: "Brave and prosperous" — also called Solo, after the Bengawan Solo river.
Its royal court is one of two heirs to the Mataram sultanate, the other being Yogyakarta.
Solo batik is the more restrained of the two court styles, and the city is a centre of Javanese classical arts.
pasuruan: Possibly from pasuruhan, a place of command or assembly.
It was a major sugar port under the Dutch.
It is the gateway to Mount Bromo, which sits in a sea of volcanic sand.
cilacap: Of Javanese origin, possibly from a word for a marshy place.
It has the only deep-water port on Java’s south coast and a large refinery.
Nusakambangan island off it holds Indonesia’s highest-security prisons.
kediri: From Sanskrit or Javanese kadiri, "to stand" or "self-standing".
It was the capital of a kingdom in the 1000s and 1100s whose court produced major Javanese literature.
Gudang Garam, one of the world’s largest clove cigarette makers, is based here.
malang: From a Javanese word meaning to obstruct or lie across.
It sits at 450 m and was a Dutch colonial retreat, with art deco streets still intact.
Its people use an inverted slang, boso walikan, in which words are said backwards — Malang becomes Ngalam.
singaraja: "Lion king" — from a palace built in 1604 by a king who took that title.
It was the Dutch capital of Bali and the island’s main port until the 1930s.
Its Gedong Kirtya holds thousands of lontar palm-leaf manuscripts, the only such library in the world.
jember: Its carnival is one of the largest costume parades in the world, staged on a 3.6 km stretch of street.
It is a tobacco region, growing cigar wrapper leaf exported to Germany and the Netherlands.
mataram: Named for the Mataram sultanate of Java, though the city is on Lombok.
It is the capital of West Nusa Tenggara and sits below Mount Rinjani.
Balinese rulers held Lombok for two centuries, which is why the town has Hindu temples alongside mosques.
denpasar: "North of the market" — den north, pasar market.
It is the capital of Bali and its largest city, though most visitors stay elsewhere on the island.
The 1906 puputan here was a ritual mass suicide of the royal court in the face of Dutch guns.
kupang: From a local chief’s name, Koepan.
Captain Bligh reached here in 1789 after 47 days in an open boat following the Bounty mutiny, having sailed 6,700 km.
It is the capital of East Nusa Tenggara and the closest Indonesian city to Australia.
